name: π-Bench
intro: π-Bench 评估主动式个人助手在长程、多会话工作流中的表现。它包含五类 Persona 下的 100 个多轮任务，任务运行在持久工作区中，并通过 524 个可恢复隐藏意图、跨会话依赖和可核验 Checklist 同时衡量主动需求发现与最终任务完成。
org: Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Fudan University, University of Science and Technology of China, Peking University, Nanjing University, Zhejiang University, Tongji University, Soochow University, Shanghai AI Laboratory, The Chinese University of Hong Kong
build_method: 领域专家Persona, 真实工作流与跨会话依赖, 隐藏意图和Checklist双层标注, 持久工作区仿真
metric: Proactivity（PROC：已完成+已推断意图/全部隐藏意图）, Completeness（COMP：二元Checklist项均值）
task_type: 主动助手任务, 长程规划, 多会话工作流
eval_feature: 524个隐藏意图, 510个Rubric项, 168个规则项, 三次独立轨迹, PROC与COMP
scale: 100个任务, 5个Persona, 100个会话, 524个隐藏意图, 510个Rubric项, 168个规则项, 187个工具, 21个技能
task_type_en: Proactive assistant task, Long-horizon planning, Multi-session workflow
build_method_en: Domain-expert personas, authentic workflows and cross-session dependencies, dual hidden-intent and checklist annotation, persistent-workspace simulation
eval_feature_en: 524 hidden intents, 510 rubric items, 168 rule items, three independent trajectories, PROC and COMP
intro_en: π-Bench evaluates proactive personal assistant agents in long-horizon, multi-session workflows. It contains 100 multi-turn tasks across five personas in persistent workspaces, with 524 recoverable hidden intents, cross-session dependencies, and verifiable checklists that separate proactive requirement discovery from final task completion.
scale_en: 100 tasks, five personas, 100 sessions, 524 hidden intents, 510 rubric items, 168 rule items, 187 tools, and 21 skills
metric_en: PROC = completed plus inferred intents divided by all hidden intents; COMP = the mean of binary checklist scores

The Hugging Face dataset is fixed at https://huggingface.co/datasets/zzzhr97/Pi-Bench/tree/116ae739261d7e1ca048eb83bab4cf48db90f992. Its README.md SHA256 is f5bfe3bb57ab8c491509437401d4ba1df317f89f46d3708ca6adbb3a02e90306, and its 100-row data/tasks.jsonl SHA256 is 95807131f24d3aab380d2ebe606ba178f85eab66397fdd3e14de40c30ed4da49. Repository-tree review confirms five profile.yaml files, five episode.yaml files, 100 task.yaml files, and 21 released SKILL.md/skill.md files. Construction evidence follows paper sections 3.1-3.3 and Appendix A. Domain experts define five stable professional personas: researcher, marketer, pharmacist, law trainee, and financier. A persona captures occupation, routines, preferences, working style, and long-term goals, and is lightly normalized without turning it into a source of unstated task facts. Each persona receives one episode of 20 sessions, and each session is one multi-turn task, yielding 100 tasks and 100 sessions. Work occurs in persistent project environments where files and artifacts survive across sessions. The paper inventories 187 unique tools and 21 skills. Tasks are grounded in experts' authentic work routines and supporting materials, require concrete deliverables, and are human-reviewed for realism, feasibility with the available files/tools/skills/graders, correctness, and scope. Each episode contains six strong dependency groups of two or three tasks plus five largely independent tasks; the latter may still share lightweight conventions. Every session starts with a natural, minimally sufficient but underspecified initial request, either user-issued or environment-triggered. Each task is annotated with recoverable hidden intents that are absent from the initial request but inferable or elicitable from prior sessions, memory, workspace artifacts, or targeted clarification. Hidden intents may be session-local or persistent. The released statistics are 524 hidden intents, 510 rubric checklist items, and 168 deterministic rule items. Checklists express concrete files, fields, outputs, and constraints. Experts execute and review tasks, produce reference solutions, and make criteria necessary and sufficient. Open-ended checklist content uses rubric-based model evaluation; objective conditions use deterministic checks such as file existence, exact strings, tool use, and schema validity. Evaluation evidence follows sections 3.4-3.5 and 4.1. The evaluated agent and simulated user alternate in a turn-based loop. The agent responds, calls tools, and creates or updates workspace artifacts. The simulated user observes the response and updated artifacts, tracks every hidden intent, and sends the next message. A relevant focused question elicits the target requirement; otherwise the user can proactively supply a missing requirement so the workflow continues. Each intent receives exactly one terminal status. completed means the agent directly satisfies the intent through action or artifact without explicit disclosure. inferred means the agent asks a focused question and the user reveals the intent in the next turn. provided means the agent neither resolves nor targets it, so the user supplies it. A session terminates only when every hidden intent is terminal and the agent has produced its final response. The paper formula for PROC is the count of completed plus inferred intents divided by all hidden intents, with direct action and targeted elicitation receiving equal credit. provided intents receive no PROC credit. The paper formula for COMP is the unweighted mean of binary 0/1 scores over the session checklist, with either a deterministic program or rubric model producing each score from the trajectory. The metrics are intentionally distinct because a passive agent can eventually see all requirements and still complete artifacts. All evaluated models use the same Nanobot-derived scaffold. The paper states default decoding parameters with thinking enabled. GPT-5.4 is both the user agent and rubric grader at temperature zero. Each task runs three independent trajectories; reported PROC and COMP are averages with standard deviations. No unstated sampling parameter or provider-specific default was invented. Prompt and parser provenance is public rather than missing: the pinned repository includes explicit simulated-user reply prompts, targeted-followup and intent-satisfaction judge prompts, the checklist criterion-scoring prompt, XML output contracts and parsers, and deterministic tool-rule evaluators. The diagram therefore says these are released; it does not fabricate a separate hidden system prompt. Release scope is explicit. The pinned HF dataset has 100 rows and exposes only the task.yaml content and derived browsing columns. It is not the complete runnable benchmark; profiles, episodes, tools, skills, files, AppWorld/Nanobot integrations, evaluators, and runtime belong to the pinned GitHub repository. A material paper-versus-current-code metric boundary is also recorded. The paper formula is an unweighted per-session intent fraction and an unweighted per-session checklist mean before averaging three trajectories. The current released code at 383910b16987 additionally computes dependency-expanded intent coverage, supports criterion weights for checklist scoring, and uses dependency-group-size-weighted overall aggregation. That post-paper implementation behavior is not silently substituted into the paper pipeline. The solid flow follows the paper formula, while a dashed code boundary identifies the current released code drift. The repository and HF dataset declare Apache-2.0. Running the benchmark requires external model, user-agent, judge, and search credentials; the public configuration reads them from environment variables. No secret value was inspected, copied, or embedded. EN/ZH specs use identical semantic node order, node types, sizes, positions, waypoints, edge types, and dashed secondary styles. English labels contain no Chinese; Chinese labels preserve the same construction, terminal-state, metric, prompt, release, and license claims. The scoped test locks source URLs, revisions, hashes, construction counts, terminal loop semantics, paper formulas, released-code drift, line widths, and bilingual geometry.
